Promotion mistakes: ❌ Technical expertise alone ↳ Don't promote exclusively on technical skills ↳ Teamwork and empathy are equally important ❌ Superficial charisma ↳ Charisma helps in the interviews - remember that ↳ Make teamwork non-negotiable ❌ Political manoeuvring ↳ Don't promote those who value politics over teamwork ↳ You will be just another obstacle in their way ❌ Short-term focus ↳ Never promote based on short-term goals ↳ People are not just resources ❌ Boss pleaser ↳ Some cultures reward pleasing your boss over results ↳ Never allow this to blind your judgement Promotion success strategies: ✅ Mentors ↳ Promote those who invest in others ✅ Trustworthy ↳ Chose those who lift others up, instead of themselves ✅ Ethical ↳ Be the ethical example for the team to follow ✅ Inclusive ↳ Encourage and value diverse perspectives ✅ Team players ↳ Encourage collaboration - it's not a zero-sum game Be the leader you wish you had. Douglas Noll

### Douglas Noll

8mo

Sébastien Bervoets reposted this

VP of Engineering. 50 developers. 4 resignations this quarter. All senior. All critical to the roadmap. Exit interviews say "better opportunity." Nobody mentions what's really happening. His solution? Equity refreshers. Remote flexibility. Innovation time. Nothing worked. Why? He was solving the wrong problem. The real issue: Emotional contagion from leadership to ICs. VP pressure from board → Terse standups → Engineering managers absorb stress → Developers feel like ticket machines → Quiet quit → Then actually quit A vicious cycle bleeding his best talent. Here's what tech leaders miss: Your developers' brains are in constant threat assessment. Shifting priorities + unrealistic sprints + zero emotional recognition = Nervous systems on fire. Every "We just need to ship this" registers as: My concerns don't matter here. That feeling compounds. Sprint after sprint. Until the LinkedIn DMs get answered. One adjustment changed everything: Engineering managers learned to say: "You're frustrated that the priorities changed again" "You feel like your technical concerns aren't being heard" "You're worried this architecture won't scale" Not "That's just how it is" or "Let's focus on solutions." Just precise emotional recognition. 𝟵𝟬 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿: - Zero senior departures - Sprint velocity up 23% - 1:1s actually productive - Glassdoor reviews? Finally honest—in a good way The engineering manager who pushed back hardest? Now runs leadership development for the entire org. "Doug, we ship code here, not feelings," he said. "Exactly," was my reply. "But feelings ship your developers. And your developers ship the code." Tech isn't about stock options and ping pong tables. It's about the humans writing the code. Acknowledge the human, keep the team shipping. Because you can't equity-refresh your way past emotional neglect.
